Where this week's projections come from

Each player's number blends, where he has one from each:

  • our model and ESPN's projection, 50% and 50%, measured on 813 graded games;
  • the betting market's implied points, 40% where books price him -- none in this week's numbers yet: books post a game's props a day or two before kickoff, the Sunday-morning run buys them, and a refresh spends no credits, so it uses only props already bought;
  • the FantasyPros consensus projection, 40% (11 of your 14 players), measured on 580 graded games.

Each weight is the one that would have been most accurate on this season's finished games, pulled toward its starting value until enough are graded. The same numbers set the lineup, P(win), this week's pickups and streams, and this week's part of every title-odds number on the page: waiver adds and drops, trades, the roster. Season values move 39% of the way toward the FantasyPros rest-of-season consensus (measured on 492 graded games), and every season-long number uses them.

Consensus projections and rankings: analysis based on data from FantasyPros.

Waiver moves, by title odds

Each pickup is priced in P(win the title) on the same simulated seasons: claiming now, against waiting and claiming only if he breaks out (you win that claim when your priority beats the other managers who also want him), less what your waiver priority is worth on future claims. Passing is not free: if he breaks out, a rival claims him, and what that does to your title odds is counted. Each move is priced on its own; make one, then refresh. Assumes about a third of active managers chase any one breakout. Injured free agents are priced as IR stashes: no roster spot until he is back, with the chance he never is.

Waiver moves, by title odds

Each pickup is priced in P(win the title) on the same simulated seasons: claiming now, against waiting and claiming only if he breaks out (you win that claim when your priority beats the other managers who also want him), less what your waiver priority is worth on future claims. Passing is not free: if he breaks out, a rival claims him, and what that does to your title odds is counted. Each move is priced on its own; make one, then refresh. Assumes about a third of active managers chase any one breakout. Injured free agents are priced as IR stashes: no roster spot until he is back, with the chance he never is.

No free agent raises your title odds enough to be worth a move.

Waiver plans: several moves together

Moves interact -- two backs chasing one lineup spot are worth less together, two dead roster spots turned into a starter and his handcuff can be worth more -- so every combination of two or three pickups and drops is screened, and the best priced in title odds against standing pat and against the best single move. Make the plan when it beats that single move by more than the simulation noise; a close call when by less.

No plan beats the best single move; make that one and refresh.

Trades

Every 1-for-1, 2-for-1 and 1-for-2 with every team, and 2-for-2 among each side's eight most valuable players; when a deal frees one of your roster spots, the free agent who adds most fills it and is priced in. For you: priced in title odds for both teams on the same simulated seasons as the waiver moves. For him: he cannot see this tool, so his side is judged the way the market values players -- the platform's projection, a player's name and last season, this season so far, injuries -- in the proportions measured from Yahoo's rostership, plus whether he gets the best player in the deal and how active he is. The yes-chance ranks offers; it is a rough estimate, not a measured rate. Each trade is priced on its own, as an alternative to the others.

By expected gain: the chance he says yes times the title odds you gain.
